name: Shield of Achilles
material: Bronze, tin, gold, silver with enamelled core
powers: Depicts the whole cosmos: earth, sea, sky, two cities, war, peace, and the encircling Ocean; impenetrable in battle.
description: The great shield Hephaestus forged for Achilles in the Iliad, the poem's supreme example of the god-smith's craft and the model of the cosmic artifact in Greek epic. Five metal layers of bronze, tin, gold and silver carry scenes of the whole world: earth, sea and sky with sun, moon and stars, two cities, one at peace with weddings, lawsuits and dance, one besieged in war, fields ploughed by oxen, a ripe harvest, a vineyard, a cattle raid with lions, and a choir of dancers, all encircled by the stream of Ocean. Homer describes its making at length when Thetis visits Hephaestus, and the finished shield mirrors the mortal world Achilles is about to leave; the passage became the defining example of ekphrasis, a poem describing a work of art. The motif was imitated in the Shield of Heracles and in Virgil's Roman answer, and it remains the archetype of the hero's world-in-miniature, an object whose decoration, not its metal, gives it power.

name: Robe of Medea
material: Robed cloth and a golden diadem, steeped in poison
powers: Bursts into flame on the wearer; destroys Glauce and her father Creon.
description: The poisoned robe and golden diadem Medea sent as bridal gifts to Glauce, Jason's new bride at Corinth; when the princess put them on, the dress burst into flames and consumed her, and her father Creon died as well when he tried to save her. Euripides makes the gifts the engine of his tragedy, delivered by Medea's own children, and the horror lies in how the objects of a wedding, the robe and crown meant to adorn a bride, become instruments of death. The motif recurs in Greek myth, most closely in the robe of Deianeira in Sophocles' Trachiniae, which destroys Heracles, and the poisoned garment became a stock 'deadly gift' of folklore, whose touch burns the wearer. Later sources expand Medea's revenge to the killing of her own sons, while the robe itself stands for the vengeance a scorned woman can take through the very language of gifts and kinship. The tale is the classic warning that a bride's finery can carry a bride's doom.

name: Bridle of Bellerophon
maker: Brought by Athena in a dream
powers: Tamed the winged horse Pegasus so Bellerophon could ride it against the Chimera.
description: The golden bridle Athena gave the Corinthian hero Bellerophon to tame the winged horse Pegasus, the instrument that let him ride the stallion and, mounted, destroy the fire-breathing Chimera of Lycia. Apollodorus records the dream in which Athena brought the bridle to Bellerophon as he slept at her altar, and the hero woke with the gift in his hand; later tellings place the meeting at the spring of Peirene on Corinth's acropolis. The bridle is an emblem of god-given mastery over a divine beast, and Pegasus, once bridled, served the hero through the trials laid on him by King Iobates, including the slaying of the Chimera. Pausanias reports that the bridle was preserved and dedicated in a temple of Athena Chalinitis, 'the Bridler', at Corinth, a relic claiming to be the very object of the legend. Its story shows how a seemingly small tool, a horse's bit, becomes the pivot of a hero's fate.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Wings of Daedalus
material: Feathers bound with wax and thread
powers: Carried Daedalus and Icarus off Crete; deadly when the wax melts in the sun's heat.
description: The feathered wings the craftsman Daedalus built with wax and thread to escape the labyrinth of Crete with his son Icarus, the most famous image of doomed invention in Greek myth. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives the fullest telling: Daedalus warns Icarus to fly neither too low, where the sea soaks the feathers, nor too high, where the sun melts the wax, but the boy exults in flight, rises, and falls into the sea that took his name, the Icarian. The wings were the answer to King Minos' prison of the labyrinth, and their construction, each feather set in order like a real bird's wing, shows Daedalus' art at its highest and most tragic. In later legend the flight is sometimes said to have ended in Sicily, where Daedalus found refuge with King Cocalus. The melting wing has become the standing warning against hubris and against exceeding the limits of human craft, and the tale endures in the proverb 'don't fly too close to the sun'.

name: Bow of Odysseus
material: Polished wood with horn tip (gift of Iphitus)
maker: Given to Odysseus by Iphitus; strung only by its owner
powers: Shot an arrow through twelve axe heads; brought death to the suitors of Ithaca.
description: The great bow of Odysseus, which no other man could string and which he alone could drive an arrow through all twelve axe heads, stands at the centre of the final test of the Odyssey. Penelope sets the contest of the bow for her suitors at Ithaca, and when the strongest of them fail even to bend it, the disguised Odysseus takes the weapon, strings it effortlessly, shoots through the axes, and then turns it on the suitors, slaughtering them with the help of his son and his faithful servants. The poem relates that the bow was a gift from Iphitus, a token of their friendship given in youth, and it had been left at home in Ithaca when Odysseus sailed for Troy, so that it keeps its place as the symbol of the household and its absent master. Its unyielding curve measures the hero's identity: only the true master of the house can draw it. The bow remains the emblem of Odysseus' patient cunning and of the return that restores order to Ithaca.

name: Crown of Ariadne
powers: Set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis after Ariadne's death.
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when she helped Theseus escape the labyrinth of Crete after he slew the Minotaur, and the circlet Dionysus later set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis. In Catullus' Carmen 64 the crown is the gift that marks Ariadne's fate after Theseus abandons her on Naxos, where Dionysus finds her and raises her crown to heaven in her honour; Apollodorus also preserves the tradition of the celestial setting. Different sources make Hephaestus or Dionysus its maker, and its gems were said to shine with a brightness of their own in the night sky. The seven bright stars of Corona Borealis still carry her name, and the crown is a standing emblem of the abandoned bride turned into a celestial monument. In Renaissance and later art the corona of Ariadne appears again and again, marrying astronomy and myth in a single golden ring of stars.

name: Shield of Aeneas
powers: Shows the future of Rome, from Romulus to the triumph of Augustus at Actium.
description: The shield Vulcan, the Roman Hephaestus, forged for Aeneas at the request of his mother Venus, engraved with the future of Rome and described at length at the close of the eighth book of the Aeneid. Its bronze bears the city's destiny: the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabine women, Rome's kings, the defence against the Gauls, the punishment of the conspirator Catiline, and the sea battle of Actium with Augustus triumphing over Antony and Cleopatra, all framed within scenes of the empire that was to come. The ekphrasis deliberately answers the Shield of Achilles in Homer: where Achilles' shield shows the whole cosmos and mortal life, Aeneas' shows a single people's ordained future. The shield is the emblem of Roman destiny made visible in metal, and the image of Aeneas lifting onto his shoulder a shield whose glory he does not understand closes the poem's first half. It remains the classic portrait of a nation reading itself in its own artifacts.

name: Sibylline Books
powers: Prophetic verses consulted by the Roman state to avert calamities; their burning punished Tarquin's haggling.
description: The nine books of prophetic verses the Cumaean Sibyl offered to the Roman king Tarquin, of which she burned six when he refused her price and sold the last three for the full amount of the original nine; Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus record the story. The surviving books, written originally on palm leaves, were kept in the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitol and were consulted only by the state, through the priestly board of the quindecimviri, at moments of grave public danger, plague, or portent, when their verses prescribed the sacrifices and rites that might turn aside the disaster. The books were thus an oracle without a voice, opened only by decree of the Senate. They were destroyed in the burning of the Capitol in 83 BC and only partially reconstructed, and their loss is itself a legend. The tale of the Sibyl's burning books became the emblem of a state that haggles with prophecy and pays the price.
source: Livy, History of Rome; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities

name: Lituus of Romulus
powers: Marked the regions of the sky for augury at Rome's foundation; found unharmed after the burning of the Curia Saliorum.
description: The lituus of Romulus was the curved augur's staff with which, in Roman tradition, Rome's founder marked out the regions of the sky when he took the auspices that sanctioned the building of the city. The relic was kept among the sacred gear of the Salian priests in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, and Cicero, Plutarch, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus record how it was found unharmed after the building burned, a survival read as a portent that the augural science, and with it Rome's favour with the gods, would endure. The lituus, a crook-like staff, was the professional badge of the augur, used to trace the templum, the sacred area of the sky, before any public act, and its shape became the pattern of the augur's staff in all later Roman state ritual. The Romulus relic belongs with the ancile and the fire of Vesta among the talismanic objects on which Rome's continuance was thought to hang. No such staff survives; the legends are our only record of it.
source: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Camillus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus

name: Ancile
maker: Fell from heaven in the reign of Numa; copies made by the smith Mamurius Veturius
powers: Pledge of Rome's eternity; twelve copies kept the true shield hidden from thieves.
description: The ancile was the sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, and was kept as a pledge that the city would rule the world as long as the shield was preserved. Fearing theft, Numa had the smith Mamurius Veturius make eleven identical copies, so that the twelve shields carried in procession by the Salian priests could not be told apart, and the legend adds that Mamurius asked as his only reward that his name be sung in the Salian hymn. Plutarch, Ovid in the Fasti, and Servius all tell the story, and the Salii struck the bronze ancilia with staffs as they danced through the city each March at the opening of the campaigning season. The shield thus joined the palladium and the fire of Vesta among the pignora imperii, the tokens of Rome's eternity. Its name passed into later usage as a word for any safeguard of the state.
source: Plutarch, Life of Numa; Ovid, Fasti (Book 3); Servius, on the Aeneid

name: Golden Bough
maker: Hidden in the wood of Proserpina
powers: Admitted a living man into the underworld; the offering Proserpina required of Aeneas.
description: The golden bough is the branch Aeneas must pluck before he may enter the underworld, the passport of his descent in the sixth book of the Aeneid. The Sibyl of Cumae tells him the bough grows in a dark wood, is of gold like mistletoe in midwinter, and can only be plucked if Fate allows: no human strength can break it, but if the Fates consent it yields at the touch, and it is the gift that Proserpina, queen of the dead, demands before any living man may pass the gate of Dis. Aeneas finds the bough on the tree, plucks it, and carries it down through the underworld, leaving it at last on the threshold of Proserpina's palace. The bough has been read since antiquity as an image of initiation, secrecy, and the crossing of death's threshold. Frazer made it the title and organizing symbol of his great study of myth and ritual, and it remains one of the most suggestive objects in classical poetry.

name: Arrows of Cupid
powers: The golden arrow kindles love; the blunt leaden one drives love away.
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses are of two kinds: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away, and the pair together explain the passions of gods and mortals alike. When Apollo taunts Cupid about his bow, the boy shoots the golden arrow into Apollo and the leaden into the nymph Daphne, so that the god burns with desire while she flees him in terror, and the chase ends only when Daphne is changed into the laurel tree. The two arrows turn love and rejection into a kind of physics of the heart, a divine mechanism behind human obsession and coldness alike. The imagery was taken up endlessly in Renaissance and Baroque art, where a gold-tipped and a lead-tipped shaft dangle from Cupid's quiver. The motif survives in the everyday phrase 'arrows of love' and in Cupid's double quiver as the emblem of love's cruelty and arbitrariness.

name: Sword of Damocles
maker: Hung at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse
powers: Showed Damocles the peril hidden in royal ease; the emblem of insecurity in power.
description: The sword of Damocles, suspended by a single horse-hair over the head of the courtier Damocles at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse, is the object by which Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations, taught that royal power is bought with anxiety. When Damocles envied the tyrant's happiness, Dionysius seated him at a banquet served in gold and silver and had him look up to find a gleaming sword hanging by a hair above his neck; the pleasure of the feast turned to dread, and Damocles understood that the ruler lives each moment under the threat of death. The image, which some ancient writers trace to still earlier tellings, became the universal emblem of the peril hidden in high place, of fortune's insecurity and the price of power. It survives in daily language wherever a 'sword of Damocles' is said to hang over an enterprise, a reputation, or a life. No such object ever existed; its whole force is in the image.

name: Corona Civica
material: Oak leaves (holm, esculent, or common oak)
powers: Rewarded a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; granted lifelong honour and the right to sit with senators.
description: The corona civica, the civic crown of oak leaves, was Rome's highest honour for a citizen soldier, awarded to the man who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground where he did it; Pliny the Elder in the Natural History and Aulus Gellius in the Attic Nights describe its rules. Woven from holm, esculent, or common oak, it was granted by the rescued man himself, who was bound to honour his saviour as a parent, and the crown carried with it the right to wear it for life, to sit with the senators at the games, and to be free of many burdens; its inscription 'ob cives servatos', 'for saving citizens', became the slogan of imperial beneficence. Pliny records that it was counted second only to the grass crown, the corona obsidionalis, in the scale of Roman decorations, and Julius Caesar and later emperors displayed it with pride. The oak crown remained a political symbol of protection down to the end of the empire.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Book 16); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights (Book 5)

name: Liver of Piacenza
powers: Model of a sheep's liver used in hepatoscopy; its sixteen inscribed zones map the heavens onto the organ.
description: The Piacenza liver, a life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver found in 1877 near Gossolengo in the countryside of Piacenza and dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BC, is the most important surviving document of Etruscan divination. Its convex upper surface is divided into sixteen inscribed zones, each naming a deity or region of the sky, and its outer edge is marked out in sectors, mapping the heavenly templum onto the organ of sacrifice. Etruscan haruspices read the future from the form, markings, and lobes of a sacrificial animal's liver, and the model, with its ritual vocabulary of gods and boundaries, served both as a teaching instrument and as a working reference for the practice. It now stands in the Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese in Piacenza, and parallels from Mesopotamia show the antiquity of the tradition. The liver is the concrete remains of a priestly science that Rome borrowed and then let die.
source: Archaeological find (Gossolengo, 1877; Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese, Piacenza)

name: Pyrgi Gold Plaques
maker: Dedicated by Thefarie Velianas of Caere
powers: Bilingual dedicatory texts linking the Etruscan goddess Uni with the Phoenician Astarte; cornerstone of Etruscan language study.
description: The Pyrgi plaques, three thin sheets of gold found in 1964 at Santa Severa, the site of the Etruscan port of Pyrgi north of Rome, bear the earliest known bilingual text in Etruscan and Phoenician and are dated to about 500 BC. They record that Thefarie Velianas, ruler of the great Etruscan city of Caere, dedicated a temple, its sacred precinct, and a shrine to the Etruscan goddess Uni, identified in the Phoenician version with Astarte, in the third year of his rule, an offering that testifies to the close religious and commercial links between Etruscan Caere and the Phoenician world of the western Mediterranean. The long Etruscan text and the shorter Phoenician version together gave scholars a rare bilingual key to the Etruscan language, and the plaques are among the oldest historical documents from Italy. They are now in the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia in Rome. The find reshaped understanding of Etruscan religion and of Caere's place in the Mediterranean network of the sixth century BC.
source: Archaeological find (Pyrgi, Santa Severa, 1964; Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome)

name: Tizona
material: Iron and steel blade with silver-gilt hilt
maker: Blade of Andalusian manufacture, c. 11th century
powers: Sword of El Cid won from King Yucef of Valencia; 'worth a thousand marks of gold' in the Cantar.
description: Tizona is the sword the Cantar de Mio Cid names as El Cid's great blade, 'worth a thousand marks of gold', which the poem says he won from King Yucef of Valencia and later demanded back from the Infantes de Carrión after they had disgraced it. The sword kept at the Museo de Burgos has a straight double-edged blade of the 11th century, of high-carbon steel with a fuller, whose metal was studied by the Universidad Complutense de Madrid in the 1990s and confirmed as forged in the hero's era, from iron probably of Sierra Morena or northern Morocco; the Gothic hilt and the acid-etched inscriptions, 'Io soi Tizona fue fecha en la era de mille quarenta' and 'Ave Maria gratia plena Dominus mecum', are later additions of the 15th-16th century. The claim that it was El Cid's rests on legend and later provenance rather than on contemporary proof. Declared a national treasure in 2003 and bought by the Junta de Castilla y León in 2007, the blade remains the most iconic object connected with the Cid.
source: Cantar de Mio Cid; Museo de Burgos (provenance and metallurgical studies)

name: Chest of El Cid
powers: A ruse: sand offered as treasure to raise funds from the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas.
description: The chest of El Cid is the wooden coffer, bound with iron, that the exiled hero in the Cantar de Mio Cid fills with sand and pawns to the moneylenders Raquel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of gold, to raise the funds his banishment has denied him. The poem has El Cid swear the chest is full of pure gold, and the lenders accept it on his word, never daring to open it, and the ruse lets the hero mock the greed of the Jews while financing his campaign; the joke is that the treasure is worthless sand and the bargain is never meant to be redeemed. The episode, told with wry comedy, is one of the most famous of the epic, showing the hero's resourcefulness and his contempt for those who trust appearances. It is a literary invention with no historical basis, and no such chest is known to have existed. The chest remains a stock image of the confidence trick that passes off worthlessness as wealth.

name: Santo Caliz
material: Agate cup with gold mounts, pearls, and gems
era: Agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC; mounts medieval
maker: Unknown Hellenistic or Roman lapidary; goldwork by later craftsmen
powers: Venerated as the cup of the Last Supper; its identification is tradition, not verified history.
description: The Holy Chalice of Valencia, an agate cup of the 2nd or 1st century BC set in medieval gold mounts with pearls and gems, is venerated in the Cathedral of Valencia as the cup of the Last Supper. The lower bowl is a genuine ancient stone vessel; the goldwork, stem, and handles are medieval, and the cup has been documented at Valencia since 1437, after being kept at Huesca and, by tradition, brought from Jerusalem to Rome and then to Spain. The identification rests on tradition rather than on any contemporary evidence, and scholars dispute the whole chain of custody, so it is more honest to call it a relic claimed as the Grail than the Grail itself. An archaeological study by Antonio Beltrán in 1960 dated the agate bowl to the late Roman Republic, confirming the antiquity of the stone but not the Christian legend. The chalice remains a focus of pilgrimage and the chief Spanish claimant among the many vessels said to be the Holy Grail.
source: Valencia Cathedral tradition; A. Beltran, archaeological study (1960)

name: Rooster of Barcelos
material: Legendary roast fowl; modern ceramic replicas
powers: A roasted rooster rose and crowed to prove a condemned pilgrim's innocence.
description: The Rooster of Barcelos comes from the Portuguese legend of a Galician pilgrim who, condemned to hang for a theft he did not commit, stood before the judge's table and swore his innocence by a roasted rooster, declaring that the bird would crow if he were innocent. As the noose was being fitted, the roast cock rose on the table and crowed; the pilgrim was freed, and he returned to Barcelos to raise a monument in thanks. The story, told in many collected versions in northern Portugal, is usually set at Barcelos on the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela, and some versions place it at the neighbouring parish of Barcelinhos. From the legend the painted ceramic rooster, the Galo de Barcelos, became the national symbol of Portugal and the country's most characteristic souvenir. The tale belongs to the wide family of miracle-of-the-roast-cock legends found across Europe, here fused with the cult of Saint James and the pilgrims' road.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; collected versions of the Barcelos legend

name: Nau Catrineta
era: Folk era (legend set in the Age of Sail)
powers: Lost at sea until an angel saved the captain and the ship reached port.
description: The Nau Catrineta is the legendary ship of the great Portuguese romance 'A Nau Catrineta', which is lost at sea for years until the starving crew cast lots to decide who must be sacrificed to save the rest, and the lot falls on the captain-general. The devil, in the shape of the lookout or of a strange ship's boy, appears to claim his soul, but the captain, praying to the Virgin, is rescued by an angel, the demon is driven off, and the ship sails safely into port. The ballad, collected by Almeida Garrett in his Romanceiro and known in many oral versions across Portugal, Brazil, and the Portuguese islands, blends the old motif of the doomed captain with Christian redemption, and some versions soften the ending or let the captain bargain his way free. The song remains among the best-loved of the Portuguese oral tradition. The ship itself has passed into speech as a name for an ill-fated vessel, and the legend mirrors the sea's deep hold on the Portuguese imagination.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; Almeida Garrett, Romanceiro

name: Portuguese Guitar
material: Wood, metal strings (twelve strings in six courses)
maker: Developed from the English cittern in Lisbon
powers: The signature voice of fado, said to express saudade itself.
description: The Portuguese guitar is the pear-shaped twelve-string cittern with a flat back and a sharp, ringing tone that is the defining instrument of fado, the song of Lisbon. It is played with a long plectrum, its six double courses of metal strings laid over a tear-shaped body, and it developed in Lisbon in the 18th and 19th centuries from the English cittern brought by British merchants, taking on its Portuguese character in the hands of local makers such as the Machado family. In fado the guitar answers and weeps with the singer, and the idiom is often said to voice saudade itself, the untranslatable longing at the heart of the song. From Lisbon the instrument spread to Coimbra, where a larger-bodied variant with its own tuning accompanies a separate tradition of sung poetry. Though a documented instrument rather than a mythic relic, it carries Portugal's musical folklore, and its sound is instantly recognised as the voice of fado.
source: Ethnographic and musicological documentation of the fado tradition

name: Nazar Boncugu
powers: Deflects the envious gaze of the nazar (evil eye).
description: The nazar boncuğu, the blue-and-white glass bead of Turkey, is the country's most widespread protective amulet, worn as jewellery and hung in homes, cars, and workplaces, and fixed to new buildings, to ward off the evil eye. The bead, usually of blue glass with concentric white, dark blue, and black circles suggesting an eye, is made by glass blowers of the Aegean region, long centred on villages such as Görece near Izmir. The Turkish tradition treats the amulet itself as expendable: a nazar that has absorbed the envious glance is said to crack or fall, and a broken one is simply replaced with a fresh bead. The belief in the evil eye, the nazar, is ancient and Mediterranean-wide, and blue eye-amulets are documented across Anatolia for centuries. Similar amulets appear throughout the region, from the Greek mati to the Arab ayin, but the Turkish nazar boncuğu, with its distinctive glassy eye, has become a global souvenir of protection.

name: Karagoz
material: Dyed translucent leather (camel hide) on a stick
powers: Comic everyman of the shadow screen, bickering with Hacivat in plays performed behind a lit panel.
description: Karagöz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, gives its name to the traditional play performed behind a lit cotton screen with flat, articulated figures of dyed translucent camel hide worked on sticks, which cast coloured shadows as the single puppeteer, the hayali, moves them. The hero Karagöz, a bald, rough-spoken everyman, bickers endlessly with his polite, wordy friend Hacivat, and their exchanges of puns and misunderstandings drive the comedy, framed by music, song, and a stock cast drawn from the Ottoman city. Popular legend, recorded from the 17th century onward, is sometimes said to trace the form to two workers, an ironworker called Karagöz and a bricklayer or timber seller called Hacivat, whose banter halted the building of a mosque, so that the sultan had them executed and a puppeteer conjured their shadows back onto a screen. The genre was performed in Ramadan and before the sultans. It remains a living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey, inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
source: Turkish oral tradition and documented Ottoman shadow theatre

name: Talismanic Shirt
material: Cotton or linen, painted with ink and gold
powers: Worn next to the skin to shield the wearer from wounds, illness, and evil in battle.
description: The tilsimli gömlek, the talismanic shirt of the Ottoman court, is a garment painted with Qur'anic verses, magic squares, the names of the four archangels, the Seal of Solomon, and the numbers of abjad calculation, worn next to the skin under armour by sultans and princes against wounds, illness, and ill luck. The making was governed by astrology: the court astronomer fixed the wearer's auspicious hour, and the shirt was begun and finished only when the sun stood in the required sign, so that each one is a document of its owner's horoscope as well as a talisman. The earliest dated example in the Topkapı collection is the shirt of Cem Sultan, begun on 30 March 1477 and finished on 29 March 1480, made for his bid for the throne and, as the story goes, never worn, its collar never opened. About eighty such shirts survive in the palace collection, most from the 16th century. They are among the most mysterious objects of Ottoman material culture, blending piety, magic, and the science of the stars.
source: Topkapi Palace Museum collection; Tezcan, Tilsimli Gomlekler

name: Mehter Davul
material: Wooden shell with skin heads, struck with a beater
powers: Beats the rhythm of the janissary march, inspiring troops and intimidating the enemy.
description: The mehter davul is the great two-headed drum of the mehter, the Ottoman military band, struck with a heavy beater to drive the slow, thundering rhythm of the janissary march, the pulse of an army on the move. The davul, a large double-skin cylinder slung at the waist or on a strap, is played with a curved stick and a thin switch, producing the deep boom and sharp crack that set the soldiers' gait; together with the shrill zurna, the kettle-drums, and the cymbals it made the band that European observers from the 16th century described as terrifying in battle and overwhelming in its din. The mehter's music was meant both to inspire the Ottoman troops and to daunt the enemy, and it marched before the army in campaigns from the Balkans to Persia. The band was abolished in 1826 together with the Janissary corps it served, but the davul lives on in successor ensembles and in the marches still played at Turkish ceremonial occasions. It remains the emblem of Ottoman martial music.
source: Ottoman musical tradition; documentation of the mehter band

name: Gusle
material: Maple bowl, single horse-hair string, horse-hair bow
powers: Accompanied heroic epic song in the oral tradition of the southern Balkans.
description: The gusle is a single-stringed bowed instrument of the southern Balkans, a round or pear-shaped bowl of maple or other wood covered with a skin, with a single horse-hair string played with a horse-hair bow, used to accompany the chanted epic poetry of the South Slavs. The singer, the guslar, plucks or bows the one string as he recites long heroic songs of battles, outlaws, and ancestral heroes, and among Croats, Serbs, Bosnians, and Montenegrins the instrument is inseparable from the living tradition of oral epic that Milman Parry and Albert Lord made famous with their studies of formulaic composition in the 1930s. In the Croatian lands the gusle was long carried by singers of the Dinaric highlands and the coast, and it has served both as a patriotic symbol and, at times, as an instrument of political song. The one-stringed fiddle is among the simplest instruments of European folk music, yet it carries an oral tradition of exceptional depth.
source: Ethnographic documentation of the South Slavic epic tradition

name: Croatian Nosnja
material: Linen, wool, and embroidery, varying by region
powers: Carried the wearer's village, age, and marital status in its cut, colour, and embroidery.
description: The nosnja, the traditional folk costume of the Croatian regions, is worn on feast days, at weddings, and at folklore festivals, and each district had its own cut, fabric, embroidery, and colour code that told the wearer's village, age, marital state, and even family at a glance. The dress is built from linen, hemp, and wool, spun, woven, and embroidered at home, and on it appear the characteristic Croatian embroideries, from the gold-worked caps of Posavina to the red-and-black geometric designs of the Dalmatian hinterland and the ornate festive dress of Slavonia. The nosnja belongs to the wider Balkan tradition of festive clothing, but its regional variety made it, in the 19th century, a badge of national identity during the Croatian national revival. It is still made by hand and worn with pride, and the rich costumes of the folk ensembles are among the most recognisable images of Croatian folklore. It is a garment of identity rather than a single mythic object.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Croatian regional costume

name: Luzzu
era: Traditional working boat (modern form early 20th century)
maker: Maltese boatwrights, family yards at Marsaxlokk and Gozo
powers: The painted Eye of Osiris on the prow wards off the evil eye and guides the boat home.
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, carries on its prow a pair of apotropaic eyes painted on either side of the bow, an inheritance many trace to the Eye of Osiris or of Horus of the ancient Mediterranean, meant to ward off the evil eye, protect the crew, and guide the boat home to a good catch. The boats, broad-beamed and high-prowed, are built and repaired by family yards at Marsaxlokk and on Gozo, painted in reds, blues, yellows, and greens, with the eyes and often a patron saint's image or a religious motto on the bows. Though the modern luzzu form dates only from the early 20th century, the eye motif is ancient and links the boats to a seafaring world older than Malta's recorded history. The working fleet of Marsaxlokk harbour, still bright with the painted gaze, is one of the most photographed sights of the island. The luzzu stands for the persistence of a Mediterranean folk belief on the decks of modern boats.
source: Ethnographic and maritime documentation of the Maltese fishing tradition

name: Ivory Statue of Galatea
powers: Brought to life by Aphrodite at Pygmalion's prayer; became his wife.
description: The ivory statue carved by Pygmalion of Cyprus, which the sculptor loved as a living woman until Aphrodite, moved by his prayer, brought it to life as Galatea, who became his wife; Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story as the classic fable of art animated by desire. Pygmalion, disgusted by the mortal women around him, carves a maiden of such beauty that he adorns, dresses, and kisses his own work, and at the festival of Venus prays for a wife like the image; the goddess answers by warming the ivory, and the statue, turned to flesh and blood, steps into his arms. The tale is set on Cyprus, the island of Aphrodite, and later writers gave the bride her name, Galatea. It has been retold endlessly in literature and art, most famously in Shaw's Pygmalion and its musical descendant My Fair Lady, as the image of the artist remaking the beloved. The living statue remains the supreme emblem of creation and love in Western culture.

name: Caladbolg
powers: Legendary sword of Cú Chulainn, capable of slicing the head off a boar with a single stroke.
description: Caladbolg, the great sword of Irish legend, is carried in the Ulster Cycle by Fergus mac Róich, the strong-armed former king of Ulster, and in some traditions it is also the blade of Cú Chulainn, who is said to have wielded it in the great single combat against his foster-brother Ferdiad in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Its name, often translated 'hard lightning' or 'hard cleft', describes a sword of fearsome cutting power. The word is the Irish cognate of the British Caledfwlch, the sword of Arthur better known as Excalibur, which makes Caladbolg the Irish link in the family of the great legendary blades of the Celtic world. In the tale of the Feast of Bricriu the sword is counted among the marvels tested by the heroes. No historical sword bearing the name survives, so its power is entirely in the literature, and it stands for the violent, glamorous world of the sagas.

name: Hermes’ Sandals
powers: Grants the wearer winged speed and the ability to travel instantly across realms.
description: The talaria, the winged sandals of Hermes, the messenger of the gods in Greek myth, carry the wearer swift as the wind across land and sea and between the realms of mortals and gods; Homer already knows them, and in the Iliad Hermes ties on his 'ambrosial, golden' sandals before his errands. In later art the sandals are always shown with small wings at the ankles, and together with the winged cap and the caduceus they make up the messenger god's badge. They are worn not only by Hermes but by heroes and deities on his errands, and in some accounts give their speed to Perseus in his flight from the Gorgons. The talaria passed into Roman tradition as the attribute of Mercury and were revived in the Renaissance as a symbol of swiftness and eloquence. The winged shoe, with the winged hat, has become the universal shorthand for the courier of the gods.

name: Aegis
powers: Provides impenetrable protection and bears the terrifying visage of Medusa.
description: The aegis, the storm-shield of Zeus, is the awesome goatskin or bronze buckler with which the god of the Iliad terrifies armies and shakes the field of battle, and which his daughter Athena also wears in the fight; its name, from the Greek for 'goat', points to its origin as a ritual skin, though Homer treats it as a wrought shield forged by Hephaestus. Its surface bears the severed head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turns all who meet it to stone, so that the shield is as much a weapon of terror as a defence. Zeus lends the aegis to his champions and shakes it as a sign of wrath, and in Athena's hands it accompanies the goddess of war and wisdom into battle. In art the aegis appears as a scaly breastplate fringed with serpents, with the gorgoneion at its centre. The word has passed into English for any protective backing or patronage.

name: Caduceus
powers: Symbolizes negotiation and safe passage; restores harmony.
description: The caduceus, the kērykeion, is the staff of the herald carried by Hermes, the messenger god, and in Greek literature it is the token of his office, the rod with which he conducts souls to the underworld, lulls the watchful, and opens the way before him; in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the staff is given to the young god by Apollo together with the golden wand and the arts of prophecy. Its familiar form, a staff entwined by two serpents and topped with a pair of wings, is the later iconography that became standard in Roman art and was revived in the Renaissance, and through it the caduceus came to stand for commerce, negotiation, and safe passage. The same image, easily confused with the single-serpent rod of the physician Asclepius, is now widely used as a medical symbol, though the two are distinct in origin. As the badge of the eloquent envoy, the caduceus remains the emblem of diplomacy itself.

name: Ankh
powers: Symbol of life; grants vitality to the bearer.
description: The ankh, the looped cross that is the Egyptian hieroglyph for 'life', is the most recognisable of Egyptian symbols, appearing on temple walls, tomb paintings, and amulets for more than three thousand years. Shaped as a cross with a looped handle, it was carried by gods and goddesses, who hold it to the nostrils of kings and of the dead to breathe life into them, and pharaohs are shown with the ankh as the sign of the eternal life that kingship conferred. It is at once a writing sign, a sacred object, and a talisman: placed on the lips and eyes of mummies, worn as jewellery, and offered to the deceased in the scenes of the Book of the Dead. Through the Coptic Church, whose cross owes its form to the ankh, the sign became the crux ansata of Christian Egypt. It has been adopted in modern culture as a symbol of life and of the African heritage. Its meaning, simply and permanently, is life itself.

name: Scarab Amulet
powers: Protection against evil; associated with rebirth.
description: The scarab amulet is the Egyptian image of the dung beetle, carved in glazed faience, stone, or hard materials and worn or placed on the body from the Old Kingdom onward, as the emblem of the god Khepri, who rolls the sun across the sky as the beetle rolls its ball of dung. The beetle's habit of appearing from the ground was read as self-creation, so the scarab became the sign of creation and of rebirth, and from the Middle Kingdom the heart scarab, inscribed with chapter 30 of the Book of the Dead, was laid over the mummy's heart to keep it from testifying against the deceased at the judgement of the dead. Hundreds of scarabs were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, in rings, necklaces, and pectorals, and the commemorative scarabs of Amenhotep III were issued like royal bulletins. As an amulet of protection and renewal the scarab is among the most widespread objects of Egyptian material culture, and its form endured into Greek and Roman amulets.

name: Scepter of Ra
powers: Authority of the sun god; used in prayers and royal ceremonies.
description: The was-sceptre, the long staff with a forked base and a stylised animal head, is the Egyptian emblem of power and dominion, and as the sceptre of the sun god Ra it stands for the authority of the creator who orders the world. Gods are shown holding the was-staff as the sign of their rule, and kings carry it in ritual scenes to declare that they exercise the dominion the gods have given; its name is written with its own hieroglyph, and the sceptre was a fixture of temple reliefs, royal ceremony, and funerary art from the Old Kingdom onward. Its forked foot and forked head are sometimes read as the form of the Set-animal or of an antelope, and the staff is often paired with the ankh and the djed pillar in the offering scenes that cover temple walls. As the staff of Ra it passes to the pharaoh as the earthly representative of the sun god. It survives as the standard visual shorthand for divine authority in Egyptian art.

name: Jade Dragon
powers: Symbol of imperial authority and protection; believed to ward off evil spirits.
description: The jade dragon of the Han dynasty is a small, coiled dragon pendant carved from nephrite jade, found in the tombs of the Chinese aristocracy of the 2nd century BC to the 2nd century AD, where it was laid among the burial goods as a symbol of the celestial forces that governed the dead and of the soul's journey through the heavens. The dragon, the long, was the creature of the east, of rain, and of imperial power, and jade, the most precious stone of the Chinese world, was believed to preserve the body and to concentrate life-force, so that the pairing made the pendant a powerful talisman of protection and rank. The Han dragons, with their sinuous, leaping forms and spiralled bodies, are masterpieces of the lapidary's art, worked with thread-cutting saws and drills into openwork curls. The motif continued for centuries, and the jade dragon remains a symbol of Chinese imperial authority and good fortune. These pendants are among the most prized objects of Chinese art in the world's collections.

name: Yumi Bow
powers: Exceptional range and accuracy; used in court archery contests.
description: The yumi, the tall Japanese longbow, is asymmetrical, with its grip placed below the centre, a design that lets an archer shoot from horseback and from the knee without the lower limb striking the saddle or the ground; the true yumi is a composite of bamboo slats glued and bound together, often with wood and hemp, in the long tradition of the master bowyers. From the Heian period the bow was the samurai's chief weapon, and the court archery contests of the era made the yumi an instrument of ceremony and status as well as of war. The chronicles of the long-shooting contests at Sanjūsangen-dō record archers who sent arrows astonishing distances along the temple porch. The yumi's great length gives it a long draw and a strong, clean release, and it remains in use in kyūdō, the modern martial art of the bow, little changed from its medieval form. It is both a status symbol of the warrior class and a living piece of Japanese ritual.

name: Heian Court Fan
powers: Elegant signaling device; used in court dances and ceremonies.
description: The Heian court fan, the hiōgi, is the folding fan of the Japanese court of the 9th to 12th centuries, made of slender strips of cypress wood joined at the base and spread in a fan of pale wood, often painted with seasonal flowers and scenes or inscribed with poems; the folding fan itself is a Japanese invention, and these court fans were among the earliest fans to reach China and Korea. Courtiers of the Heian aristocracy used the fan to conceal the face, to gesture in the dance, to signal discreetly at court, and, in the elaborate etiquette of the age, to express shades of meaning the spoken word could not carry; in the paintings of the Tale of Genji the fan is as much a badge of rank as an accessory. Fans were also carried in the rituals of the court, held before the face in ceremony and in the kagura dance, and a painted fan was a gift that carried the giver's taste and standing. The hiōgi survives in the formal fans of Shinto ritual and in the court dance traditions of Kyoto.
